## Before the first half

Nothing new for the physics. Everything in the lecture's reproductions runs on numpy,
scipy, sympy and matplotlib.

Two of them also want **healpy**, which is the only compiled dependency anywhere in this
course:

```
conda install -c conda-forge healpy
```

If that fails, you lose `harmonic-hd-maps` and `anisotropy-prior` and nothing else — the
derivation itself is deliberately healpy-free.

## Scope

Everything today is the **Earth term only** — the correlation between two distinct pulsars.
The pulsar term is what doubles $C(0)$ from $1/2$ to $1$ for a self-correlation, and it is
uncorrelated between pulsars, so it adds a diagonal and nothing else to the curve we
compare against.

We also do not touch a real timing dataset. There are no pulsars, no timing model and no
residuals anywhere in the code: the background is built from a mass function, and the one
piece of real data is a shipped posterior. That costs the whole business of red noise and
the confusion problem, which is a genuine part of what makes PTAs hard — we pay for it in
a slide.

What it buys is a day where every number can be checked against something that did not
produce it.

---

## If something disagrees

Good. That is the assignment. Five disagreements with published values are already
documented in the reproductions — including one where our $h_c$ sits 9 % below the printed
value and nobody has explained why, and one where a gate **we** wrote turned out to be
arithmetically impossible to satisfy.

They are in each exercise's `run.log`, under the heading that says what was found and how
it was treated. Find a sixth.
